events.title: The martyrdom of Sts. Peter and Paul at Rome
events.shortBlurb: Tradition holds that the two great Apostles gave their lives at Rome under Nero, consecrating the city with their blood…
body: The earliest witness is Clement of Rome, who about the year 96 recalled how Peter and Paul had borne their testimony 'among us' and gone to their reward. Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the Romans soon after, joins their names together, and about 170 Bishop Dionysius of Corinth affirmed that both had taught in Italy and suffered martyrdom at the same time.

Their deaths fell in the persecution Nero loosed after the fire of 64. Origen relates that Peter was crucified head downward at his own plea, judging himself unworthy to die as his Lord had died; Paul, a Roman citizen, perished by the sword. About the year 200 the presbyter Gaius could point out their trophies on the Vatican hill and along the Ostian Way.

Over those trophies rose the basilicas of Saint Peter on the Vatican and Saint Paul Outside the Walls. A Roman calendar of 354 attests their joint memory on 29 June as far back as 258, and excavations beneath Saint Peter's in the 1940s uncovered the ancient monument over the grave long held to be Peter's — the rock on which the Roman Church has built.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles”

events.title: Pius IX convokes the First Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Aeterni Patris the pope summoned the first general council of the Church in three centuries…
body: On 29 June 1868, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, Pius IX published the bull Aeterni Patris, summoning the bishops of the Catholic world to the first ecumenical council since Trent had closed in 1563. The fathers were called to meet the errors of the age and to strengthen the Church's doctrine and discipline.

The council opened in St. Peter's Basilica on 8 December 1869 with some seven hundred fathers, the largest assembly of bishops the Church had seen. In April 1870 it issued the constitution Dei Filius on faith and reason, and on 18 July, in Pastor Aeternus, it defined the primacy of the Roman Pontiff and his infallibility when speaking ex cathedra.

Two months later, on 20 September 1870, Italian troops breached the walls of Rome, and on 20 October Pius IX suspended the council indefinitely. It was never reconvened, and its projected constitution on the Church and her mission was left unfinished.
